briefing.opening: Analyst, someone just posted to the whole company on Slack.

act1.title: Rebuild the timeline
act1.short: Put the evidence in the order it happened. Red herrings go to Not related.
act1.help: Drag an evidence card onto the timeline in the order it happened, or onto Not related. You can also tap a card, then use the buttons.
act1.pzHelp: Tap the timeline entry that shows the first successful access.
act1.doneHelp: Six pieces of evidence, from one accepted approval to a company-wide post.
act1.finding: Patient zero was the approval request the EXT contractor accepted. The attacker already had the password and kept trying to log in; each attempt sent a two-factor approval request, until one was accepted. From there they reached other employee accounts, got elevated permissions to G-Suite and Slack, took some internal data and posted to a company-wide Slack channel. Uber says public services stayed up and it had not seen access to production systems.

hints.1: The password was already known. What stood between the attacker and the account?
hints.2: Which log shows the first time they actually got in?
hints.3: One account is never enough. Whose accounts came next, and what rights?
hints.4: With admin rights, what did they take?
hints.5: The moment the whole company noticed: two things employees saw, in either order.
hints.6: The other half of that moment. Either order counts.

wrongLines.early: Not yet. Something else had to happen before this.
wrongLines.pz: That is not the first successful access.

timeline.text: Malware on the contractor's personal device exposed their Uber corporate password. Uber says it is likely the attacker bought it on the dark web.
timeline.why: It happened outside Uber's network, on a personal device. A password alone was not enough, though: the account also had two-factor approval.

timeline.text: The attacker repeatedly tried to log in to the contractor's account. Each time, the contractor received a two-factor login approval request, which at first blocked access.
timeline.why: The password was right. Only the approval stood in the way, and the attacker could ask for it again and again.

timeline.text: Eventually the contractor accepted one approval request, and the attacker logged in to the account.
timeline.why: The request only asked yes or no. One yes was enough.

timeline.text: The attacker accessed several other employee accounts and got elevated permissions to tools including G-Suite and Slack. Uber hasn't said how the permissions were obtained.
timeline.why: Uber hasn't published how, so the game doesn't guess. What matters: from one contractor account, the attacker reached admin-level access.

timeline.text: The attacker appears to have downloaded some internal Slack messages, accessed or downloaded information from an internal finance tool used to manage some invoices, and accessed Uber's HackerOne dashboard. Bug reports the attacker could access had been remediated.
timeline.why: With elevated permissions, internal tools hand over what they hold.

timeline.text: The attacker posted a message to a company-wide Slack channel and reconfigured Uber's OpenDNS to show a graphic image to employees on some internal sites.
timeline.why: This is where the attack became visible. Uber's existing security monitoring let its teams quickly identify the issue.

timeline.text: Uber took internal tools down as a precaution; they came back on Sept 16. Uber, Uber Eats, Uber Freight and the Driver app stayed operational.
timeline.why: Not an attacker action: Uber's own precaution while it responded. Uber says it had not seen access to production (public-facing) systems.

rewind: Now rewind. You're Uber's security team, before the first approval request. Stop it.

map.note: ATT&CK codes for each stage come from the timeline above, so Act 1 and Act 2 always match.

hidden.name: EXT contractor account signing in from an unmanaged personal device

controls.name: Number matching for employee accounts
controls.why: Employees now type the number shown on the sign-in screen, so a blind approval does nothing.
controls.whyScoped: Covered employee accounts only. The EXT contractor account wasn't in that policy, so a plain approval request still worked.
controls.teach: A policy only protects the accounts it is switched on for.

controls.name: Audit contractor (EXT) accounts: devices and MFA methods
controls.why: Found it: an EXT contractor account signing in from an unmanaged personal device, outside the employee policy.
controls.teach: Uber says malware on the contractor's personal device exposed the password.

controls.name: Extend number matching to contractor accounts
controls.why: The contractor account now asks for the number on the sign-in screen. Requests the contractor never started can’t be approved with one tap.
controls.teach: CISA recommends enabling “number matching” on MFA configurations to prevent MFA fatigue.
controls.quote: CISA recommends enabling “number matching” on MFA configurations to prevent MFA fatigue.

controls.name: Require managed devices for contractor sign-in
controls.why: Contractor accounts can only sign in from devices Uber manages. The attacker's device isn't one, so the accepted approval opened nothing.
controls.teach: Game design: Uber's update doesn't name this control.

controls.name: Alert on denied and bulk MFA requests
controls.why: A burst of approval requests on one account that weren’t approved raised an alert while it was happening.
controls.teach: CISA recommends that organizations investigate denied push notification request occurrences.
controls.quote: CISA recommends that organizations investigate denied push notification request occurrences.

controls.name: Train staff to report unexpected MFA requests
controls.why: The contractor reported the approval requests they hadn’t started.
controls.teach: CISA recommends training users to report unknown or bulk confirmation requests.
controls.quote: CISA recommends training users to report unknown or bulk confirmation requests.

controls.name: Alert on new admin permissions in G-Suite and Slack
controls.why: New elevated permissions in G-Suite and Slack raised an alert.
controls.teach: Game design: Uber hasn't said how the permissions were obtained, so this alert watches the result.

controls.name: Rotate keys to internal services
controls.why: Keys to internal services are replaced, so access the attacker may hold stops working.
controls.teach: Uber rotated keys to many internal services.

controls.name: Lock the codebase during response
controls.why: No new code changes while the response runs, so nothing new slips into the codebase.
controls.teach: Uber locked down its codebase, preventing any new code changes.

controls.name: Re-authenticate everyone when restoring tools
controls.why: Everyone signs in again when internal tools come back, so old sessions don’t carry over.
controls.teach: Uber required employees to re-authenticate when restoring access to internal tools.

controls.name: Stronger password complexity rules
controls.why: The password was bought, not guessed. A complex password works just as well once someone else has it.

controls.name: Force password expiry every 30 days
controls.why: Uber's update doesn't say how long the password was out there. A new password is just as easy for malware to steal again.

controls.name: Geo-block foreign sign-ins
controls.why: Uber's update doesn't say where the attacker signed in from. A rule built on a guess stops nothing here.

controls.name: Web application firewall on public apps
controls.why: Uber says it had not seen access to production (public-facing) systems. The attack went through internal tools.

stars.two: stopped at the entry stage (damage NONE). That needs every account type discovered first.
stars.three: ★★ plus at least one detect and one recover control in the build
stars.nextOne: ★: stop the attack at any stage.
stars.nextTwo: ★★: stop it at the entry stage. Find every kind of account before you set the policy.
stars.nextThree: ★★★: add a detect and a recover layer in case prevention fails.

act2.title: Harden sign-in
act2.short: Before the first approval request. Deploy controls on a budget, then run the real attack against your build.
act2.help: Tap a control to deploy or remove it, or drag it onto a stage in the zone it protects. Each control costs energy and the budget is 7, so you can't buy everything. Not every account is covered by your policies yet: discovery controls find what's missing. Then execute the attack: it replays stage by stage against your build, and the log explains every result.
act2.rewindButton: > REWIND TO BEFORE THE FIRST REQUEST
act2.attemptedNote: Malware on a personal device and a sale on the dark web happen outside Uber's network, so you can't block them there. Defense starts at stage 2, when the password meets sign-in.

prevented.title: Breach prevented
prevented.sub: Attack chain broken at stage {n} of {total}. The approval opened nothing.

contained.title: Breach contained
contained.sub: They got in, but you stopped them at stage {n} of {total}, before the company-wide post.

detected.title: Breach detected
detected.sub: The attack ran its course, but your detection caught it in progress.

succeeded.title: Breach succeeded
succeeded.sub: Like the real incident: elevated access, internal data taken and a post to the whole company.

tips.notStopped: The attack ran all the way. Check which accounts your sign-in policies actually cover.
tips.unknownAsset: The attacker came in through an account outside your employee policy. Find every kind of account before you set the rules.
tips.notEntry: Stopped, but only after they got in. For ★★, stop it at the entry stage.
tips.needLayers: Prevention held. For ★★★, add a layer that notices the attack and one that cleans up after it: prevent, detect, recover.
tips.decoys: {n} decoy(s) cost budget but did nothing against this attack.
tips.friction: High friction: users will push back. Find a lighter build.

always.t: Uber's real response was mostly recovery: password resets for compromised accounts, rotated keys, a locked codebase and re-authentication when tools came back.
